title: First band, its members and the repertoire
summary: He names the All-Star band members and the stock tunes and blues they played; how the banjo was played and the New Orleans banjoists he admired.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: We were playing around there, around like a million boys, and we'd play, I remember what they, that day they'd call it, Pilot Land, but that's all out there. And, well, I ended up on the other side of Gentile, Jefferson, I mean, St. Fennard Avenue, that's all built up now. You see, I was doing progression there, I remember that as well.
Who did you say was in that band?
Oh, the leader was named George Morris, a trombone player, and a trumpet player was named Thomas Mack. And Edmund Washington. We all had, we were taking lessons from this, Sam, for the Perkins. Yeah.
Oh, you were all taking lessons together?
Yeah. Oh. And we just, we called ourselves, we were practicing and trying to, you know, get ourselves familiar with playing together, see.
What kind of songs would you play?

Oh, those times when we played, well, I understand the tune of those times, like, you had to play Tiger, Egg, you had to play, I remember Bucket's got a hole in it. And, oh, they had a lack of blues, you may play in B-flat or F or something like that, you know.
How would they, how would the banjo play on that? Was it straight 4-4 or what'd you do like?

Well, it was, well, I can learn it then, I mean, I first started out playing straight 4-4, and after a while I used to listen to that banjo player like John Morrell, he was very popular and good. And the other ones, that boy named Pley, a little blackie, Santiago. Santiago. His uncle played a very nice banjo. I remember he was playing at a place called Eli Beans that was running that place then. When I was young, I used to stand on the outside and listen at him, you see. That's how I developed ideas about playing, you know, about, if none of them were trying to get an idea how the banjo should be played, see. Yeah. Yeah.
And, uh, that was, uh, most of the numbers you would play, like Tiger, Egg, and Bucket, uh.

Yeah, I see, those were the popular numbers. Yeah, the standard numbers. And then you had a little popular tune, because we all could read, and we'd buy the little stocks that thing was out, you know, you know.
That was an old reading band, you could all read?

Well, we could all read, yeah. Drummer, too? Yeah, even Joe Wynn could read. My curtain could read, yeah. But we did, like I said, we did a lot of faking and everything, yeah. And sometimes it, it, uh, you'd go and maybe get the lead part, and then you'd have to fake your cards, you know, or something like that. And then we'd go down and buy stock, you see.
